summary.text: Heredity is the passing on of genetic information from parents to their offspring.
Inherited traits are controlled by genes, and heritable traits pass from one generation to the next via DNA, a molecule that encodes genetic information.
Through heredity, genetic variations in populations can accumulate and cause species to evolve by natural selection.

items.prompt: Over many generations, a researcher cuts the tails off every mouse before it breeds. What do the newest litters look like?

options.label: They are born with shorter tails, since the loss is passed on
They are born with no tails, as the loss builds up over time
They still develop tails, because the injury isn't inherited
They develop tails only if their parents were cut late in life

items.explain: When Weismann cut the tails off many generations of mice, the offspring continued to develop tails, which showed the inheritance of acquired traits has little basis.

items.prompt: Two cousins sit in the same sun for a day. One turns brown, while the other reddens badly and never darkens. What best explains the gap?

options.label: Inherited genotype differences affect how easily they tan
The sun rewrote the genes of the cousin who turned brown
Sunlight alone decides it, with genes playing no part
The reddening cousin simply stayed out in the sun longer

items.explain: Some people tan more easily than others because of differences in their genotype, and people with albinism do not tan at all.

items.prompt: Suppose a child's traits were always an average of the two parents' traits. What would happen to the variety within a population over generations?

options.label: It would grow, because averages keep creating new extremes
It would stay the same, since averaging changes nothing
It would shrink only for the very rarest traits
It would fade in a few generations, leaving less to select

items.explain: Blending inheritance would lead to uniformity in only a few generations and remove the variation natural selection acts on.

items.prompt: A mutation changes a gene's DNA sequence and produces something new at that spot. What is the new form, and what might it do?

options.label: A new chromosome, which swaps the gene to a new position
A new allele, which may change the trait the gene controls
A new locus, which moves the trait to another parent
A new genome, which replaces every trait in the organism

items.explain: DNA sequences can change through mutations, producing new alleles, and a new allele within a gene may alter the trait the gene controls.

items.prompt: Over many generations, a species' repeated activities reshape its surroundings, and later generations grow up in them. What do descendants inherit under niche construction?

options.label: Only their genes, since surroundings are never inherited
Only the surroundings, with no genes passed on
Their genes plus the environmental features their ancestors created
Their ancestors' acquired habits, written into their DNA

items.explain: Under ecological inheritance, descendants inherit genes plus the environmental characteristics generated by their ancestors' ecological actions.

items.prompt: A critic in 1859 accepts that traits vary but asks how they pass from parent to child. What gap in Darwin's theory is she pointing at?

options.label: No underlying mechanism of heredity was known
No evidence that any traits ever varied
No explanation for why species exist at all
No fossils from earlier periods of Earth's history

items.explain: When Darwin proposed his theory in 1859, one of its major problems was the lack of an underlying mechanism for heredity.

paragraphs.heading: What heredity is
paragraphs.text: Heredity, also called inheritance, is the passing of genetic information from parents to their offspring. It can happen through sexual or asexual reproduction, as new cells form either when one cell divides or when two cells combine their genomes. The branch of biology that studies it is genetics. Heredity matters for evolution because it lets genetic differences build up in populations, so that species can change through natural selection.

paragraphs.heading: Genotype and phenotype
paragraphs.text: Eye colour in humans is an inherited trait: a child may get a brown-eye trait from one parent. Traits like this are controlled by genes, and an organism's full set of genes is called its genotype. Its phenotype is the full set of features you can observe in its body and behaviour, and these come from genotype and environment working together. So much of the phenotype is not inherited. A suntan comes from genes meeting sunlight and is not passed to children, yet people with albinism, an inherited trait, do not tan at all.

paragraphs.heading: How DNA carries it
paragraphs.text: Heritable traits travel between generations in DNA, a long molecule built from four kinds of bases. The order of those bases holds the information, much as the order of letters holds the meaning of a text. A gene is a stretch of DNA that specifies one working unit, and inside cells the long strands of DNA form compact structures called chromosomes. The exact place of a sequence on a chromosome is its locus, and when the sequence there differs between individuals, the different versions are called alleles.

paragraphs.heading: Where variation comes from
paragraphs.text: New alleles appear when mutations change DNA sequences. A mutation inside a gene can alter the trait that gene controls, and so change the phenotype. That neat link between one allele and one trait holds in some cases. Most traits, though, are more complex and depend on several genes interacting.

paragraphs.heading: Inheritance beyond genes
paragraphs.text: Some heritable changes cannot be explained by the DNA molecule acting directly. These are grouped as epigenetic inheritance, found in processes such as DNA methylation, gene silencing by RNA interference and the three-dimensional shapes of proteins such as prions. Inheritance can also work on a larger scale. Through niche construction, the repeated activities of organisms change their surroundings, so descendants inherit both genes and an environment their ancestors shaped. Cultural traits can be inherited too.

paragraphs.heading: Darwin's missing piece
paragraphs.text: Charles Darwin set out his theory of evolution in 1859, and one big gap was that he had no mechanism for heredity at the time. His own view combined two ideas: blending inheritance, and the passing on of traits acquired during life. Yet blending would make a population uniform within a few generations, leaving no variation for natural selection to act on. In the 1880s August Weismann removed the tails of mice, generation after generation, and their young still grew tails, which showed that the inheritance of acquired traits had little basis.
